William Branthwaite
wil'yam branth'wāt
n. (William Branthwaite, 1563–1619, master of Gonville and Caius and translator of the Authorized Version)
Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector; English Branthwaite, from a Cumberland place-name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

William Branthwaite was a fellow of Emmanuel College in its first Puritan generation, master of Gonville and Caius, and a member of the Second Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version. Emmanuel had been founded in 1584 expressly to train preachers, and it bred the men who would later sit in the Westminster Assembly and settle New England; Branthwaite is the link between that house and the version. He left his books to his college. The dictionary notes the combination that is easy to miss at this distance: a convinced Puritan, working under a king who disliked Puritans, on a Bible that both would use, and doing it without a rendering that favours either party (1Co 2:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Puritan as one who affected extraordinary purity in religious worship, and bequeath as to give or leave by will.

expand to see more

PU'RITAN, n. One who affected or professed extraordinary purity in the forms of religious worship, and objected to the ceremonies retained in the church.

BEQUEATH', v.t. To give or leave by will; to devise some species of property by testament.

COL'LEGE, n. In a general sense, a collection or assemblage; a society of men, set apart for learning or religion.

IM'PARTIAL, a. Not partial; not biased in favor of one party more than another; indifferent.

Modern Corruption

An Emmanuel Puritan rendering Scripture under a king who disliked Puritans.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion that every translation encodes its committee's party. The Authorized Version is the hardest case for that theory. It was produced by bishops and Puritans sitting in the same rooms under rules that forbade marginal notes of interpretation, and the result served both sides and then outlived both.

The principle to recover is that the words are the Holy Ghost's and the translator's business is to carry them, not to steer them. “Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth” (1Co 2:13). The purity claimed is the text's: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6). And Paul's own standard forbids selection: “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek didaktos (G1318), taught, instructed; Hebrew tsaraph (H6884), to refine, to try as metal.

expand to see more

Greek didaktos (G1318) — taught, communicated by teaching; 1 Corinthians 2:13.

Greek sugkrino (G4793) — to compare, to join fitly together; 1 Corinthians 2:13.

Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, to try, to purify; Psalm 12:6.

Greek hupostellomai (G5288) — to draw back, to shun, to keep silent; Acts 20:27.

Greek logion (G3051) — an oracle, a divine utterance; Romans 3:2.

Usage

"“not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth” (1Co 2:13) — bishops and Puritans in the same rooms."

"“The words of the LORD are pure words” (Psa 12:6) — no marginal notes of interpretation."

"“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — Emmanuel's first generation."
